en: The Sūtra on Adorning the Bodhicitta, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...

There was a great assembly of twelve hundred bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas—namely, the bodhisattvas Jñānaprabha, Dharmaprabha, Candraprabha, Sūryaprabha, Anantaprabha, Bhadrapāla, and the other sixteen virtuous men (*satpuruṣa*), whose practices were like those originally cultivated by Mañjuśrī;
furthermore, there were sixty bodhisattvas whose practices were like those originally cultivated by Maitreya Bodhisattva—these being the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of this Bhadrakalpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma.

Then, within the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Si Wuliangyi (Infinite Meaning). He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and scattered various precious flowers over the Buddha.
Having scattered [the flowers] over the Buddha, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a question; I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant me permission."
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Contemplating Immeasurable Meanings,
“Ask whatever you wish.
The Bodhisattva Contemplating Immeasurable Meanings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the bodhicitta?
What is this bodhicitta?”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Infinite Meaning:
“For a bodhisattva who cultivates the bodhicitta, that bodhicitta cannot be found apart from sentient beings.”
This mind is neither form nor vision, and as for phenomena, there is no one who attains them.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are empty.
The Bodhisattva Contemplating Immeasurable Meanings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The characteristics of dharmas are thus profoundly deep.”
"How should a bodhisattva practice?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Infinite Meaningful Thought: "Good son!
The bodhicitta is neither existent nor created; it is free from words and letters.
Enlightenment is itself the mind, and the mind is itself sentient beings.
If one can understand in this way, this is called a bodhisattva cultivating the bodhicitta.
Awakening is not a mind of the past, future, or present; likewise, sentient beings are not of the past, future, or present.
One who can understand in this way is called a bodhisattva.
Yet, within this, there is truly nothing to be attained; it is because there is nothing to be attained that one attains.
If one does not attain anything regarding all phenomena, this is called attaining bodhi.
For the sake of sentient beings who have newly begun their practice, it is said that there is bodhi.

Just as an arhat attains realization yet finds nothing to be obtained within the dharmas, so too is it said that there is bodhi by means of conventional terminology; however, in reality, bodhi is unobtainable.

If one finds nothing to be apprehended in all phenomena, this is called attaining bodhi. Yet within this, there is neither mind nor one who creates the mind; there is neither bodhi nor one who creates bodhi;

there are neither sentient beings nor one who creates sentient beings; there are neither śrāvakas nor those who set out as śrāvakas; there are neither pratyekabuddhas nor those who set out as pratyekabuddhas; there are neither bodhisattvas nor those who set out as bodhisattvas; there is neither Buddha nor one who becomes a Buddha; there is neither the conditioned nor one who creates the conditioned; there is neither the unconditioned nor one who creates the unconditioned. Within this, that which was attained, is being attained, and will be attained—all are unapprehendable.
The Buddha told him:
"Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
That which ought to be explained, I shall now explain:
"There are ten dharmas for a bodhisattva who generates the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
What are these ten?"
The first resolve is generated, accomplishing the root of all virtues; it is like Mount Sumeru, adorned with myriad jewels.
The second resolve is generated, practicing the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*); it is like the great earth, which nurtures and sustains all wholesome dharmas.
The third resolve is generated, practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); it is likened to the lion king, who can subdue all wild beasts because he eradicates false views.
Generating the fourth mind, one practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); it is like Nārāyaṇa’s firmness, being indestructible, because it eradicates afflictions (*kleśa*).

Generating the fifth mind, one practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); manifesting the practice of all wholesome dharmas, it is like celestial flowers that teach the Dharma according to one's wishes.
Generating the sixth mind, one practices the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); it is like the light of the sun, which eradicates all darkness.
Generating the seventh mind, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā*; all vows are fulfilled, analogous to a merchant who has escaped all perils.
Generating the eighth mind, one practices the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*; all obstacles are eliminated, analogous to the full moon, pure and free from defilement.
Generating the ninth mind, one desires to fulfill original vows, to roam through pure Buddha-lands, to delight in hearing the profound and wondrous Dharma, and to eliminate poverty.
When one gives rise to the tenth mind, its wisdom is as infinite as space, just as a wheel-turning monarch accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Good son!

One who is thus able to give rise to these ten kinds of mind is called a bodhisattva; they are also called a mahāsattva, an unconditioned being, an unobstructed being, a being who has already attained deliverance, and an inconceivable being.
Furthermore, within this, there is neither mind nor bodhi.
"Moreover, son of good family,
there are thirteen samādhis that protect and sustain the bodhicitta."

What are these ten? The first mind is generated and sustained by the *dharmaratna-samādhi*; the second mind is generated and sustained by the *dṛḍha-samādhi*; the third mind is generated and sustained by the *acala-samādhi*; the fourth mind is generated and sustained by the *avaivartika-samādhi*; the fifth mind is generated and sustained by the *ratnapuṣpa-samādhi*; the sixth mind is generated and sustained by the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi*; the seventh mind is generated and sustained by the *sarvārtha-samādhi*; the eighth mind is generated and sustained by the *jñānāvabhāsa-samādhi*; the ninth mind is generated and sustained by the *pratyutpanna-buddhasammukhāvasthita-samādhi*; and the tenth mind is generated and sustained by the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The characteristics of the first stage of a bodhisattva are able to see three thousand buddha-fields filled with billions of nayutas of hidden treasures;
the second stage is able to see three thousand buddha-fields as level and smooth, adorned with the brilliant splendor of various jewels."
On the third stage, one is able to see various powerful warriors subduing their enemies;
on the fourth stage, one is able to see wind-circles arising from the four directions, with various exquisite flowers spread across the ground;

on the fifth stage, one is able to see many female musicians adorning their bodies with various precious necklaces, their countenances graced by celestial crowns of *utpala* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *vārṣika* flowers, and *atimuktaka* flowers.

In the sixth stage, one sees various jeweled ponds filled with the eight meritorious qualities of water, their four sides lined with stairways of the seven treasures and their bottoms strewn with golden sand; one sees oneself sporting and enjoying oneself within these ponds.
In the seventh stage, one sees various hells to one's left and right, yet passes through them without any difficulty.
In the eighth stage, one sees upon both shoulders a lion king, majestic in appearance, with banners atop its head, possessing great power to subdue all other beasts.

In the ninth stage, one sees the Wheel-Turning Sage King surrounded by hundreds of thousands of ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders, transforming immeasurable sentient beings through the True Dharma, and sees various jeweled canopies suspended and covering him in the void above;
in the tenth stage, one sees the Buddha’s form-body, his body the color of pure gold emitting great radiance, as he preaches the Dharma while surrounded by a great assembly.
“Good son!
These ten kinds of correspondences should be skillfully distinguished as they bring about the accomplishment of the ten stages through the power of samādhi.
Furthermore, good son!”
On the first stage, one produces the *dhāraṇī* of superior progress;
on the second stage, the *dhāraṇī* of indestructibility;
and on the third stage, the *dhāraṇī* of peace and security.
On the fourth stage, there arises the dharani of being difficult to obstruct or destroy;
on the fifth stage, there arises the dharani of various adornments of the flowers of merit;
on the sixth stage, there arises the dharani of the perfect clarity of wisdom.
On the seventh stage, the *dhāraṇī* of the increase of birth arises;
on the eighth stage, the *dhāraṇī* of non-conceptuality arises as the foremost, with eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇīs* arising together with it;
on the ninth stage, the *dhāraṇī* of the boundless arises as the foremost, with sixty-two billion nayutas of *dhāraṇīs* arising together with it.
The *daśabhūmi-ajātadhāraṇī* arises as the foremost, and ten billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* dhāraṇīs arise simultaneously with it.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

On the first stage, one practices the perfection of giving; on the second stage, the perfection of ethical discipline; on the third stage, the perfection of patience; on the fourth stage, the perfection of vigor; on the fifth stage, the perfection of meditation; on the sixth stage, the perfection of wisdom; on the seventh stage, the perfection of skillful means; on the eighth stage, the perfection of knowledge; on the ninth stage, the perfection of maturing sentient beings; and on the tenth stage, the perfection of fulfilling all vows. In this manner, these perfections are all fully accomplished within their respective stages.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
there are ten kinds of *dānapāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these ten?

First is the faculty of faith; second is the faculty of concentration; third is great loving-kindness; fourth is great compassion; fifth is self-rejoicing; sixth is rejoicing in others; seventh is the arousal of all vows; eighth is the upholding of all sentient beings; ninth is the four means of integration; and tenth is drawing near to the teachings of all Buddhas. These are called the ten dharmas that accomplish the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
"Furthermore, son of good family,
there are ten dharmas for practicing the perfection of śīla (ethical discipline). What are these ten?

First, to be free from the eight difficulties; second, to accomplish the merits of a Buddha; third, to leave behind the stage of the śrāvaka; fourth, to leave behind the stage of the pratyekabuddha; fifth, purity of body; sixth, purity of speech; seventh, purity of mind; eighth, adorning the mind; ninth, severing the conditions for rebirth in hell; tenth, fulfilling all aspirations through practice. These ten dharmas constitute the accomplishment of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
"Furthermore, good son,
there are ten dharmas for practicing the pāramitā of kṣānti. What are these ten?

First is the power of patience; second is exultation; third is bringing sentient beings to maturity; fourth is being able to endure profound dharmas; fifth is the absence of "self" and "other"; sixth is severing anger and resentment; seventh is not cherishing the body; eighth is not cherishing life; ninth is abandoning delusion; tenth is contemplating the equality of the Dharma-body. Through these ten kinds of dharmas, one accomplishes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There are ten dharmas for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
What are these ten?

First is the faculty of diligence; second is the power of diligence; third is right effort; fourth is right mindfulness; fifth is assisting sentient beings with one’s body; sixth is following along with sentient beings through mind and speech; seventh is not retreating from one’s sphere of practice; eighth is the elimination of laziness; ninth is subduing evil associates; tenth is the accumulation of all-knowledge. These are called the ten dharmas that accomplish the *vīryapāramitā*.
"Furthermore, good son!
There are ten dharmas for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the dhyānapāramitā.
What are these ten?

First is the faculty of concentration; second is the power of concentration; third is equanimity in concentration; fourth is sporting in the various dhyānas; fifth is samādhi; sixth is the fruition of samādhi; seventh is not destroying any wholesome dharmas; eighth is the eradication of the enemies that are the afflictions; ninth is relinquishment regarding the true Dharma; tenth is the aggregate of concentration. Through these ten dharmas, one accomplishes the dhyāna-pāramitā.
"Furthermore, good son,
there are ten dharmas for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
What are these ten?

First is the faculty of wisdom; second is the power of wisdom; third is right view; fourth is right mindfulness; fifth is skillful means regarding the aggregates (*skandha*); sixth is the discernment of the elements (*dhātu*); seventh is the noble truths (*āryasatya*); eighth is unobstructed knowledge; ninth is the turning away from false views; tenth is the practice of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Through these ten dharmas, one achieves the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Furthermore, good son,
there are ten dharmas for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā). What are these ten?

First is acting in concert with sentient beings; second is sustaining sentient beings; third is great compassion; fourth is tirelessness; fifth is departing from the practices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; sixth is entering the pāramitās; seventh is discerning the capacities and dispositions of others as they truly are; eighth is supporting wholesome minds; ninth is entering the stage of non-retrogression; and tenth is subduing all māras. These are called the ten dharmas that accomplish the skillful means of the pāramitās.
"Furthermore, good son!
What is the meaning of *pāramitā*?
To practice with progressive fulfillment is the meaning of *pāramitā*; to achieve supreme wisdom is the meaning of *pāramitā*."
The meaning [of perfection] is that it does not reside in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is the meaning of *pāramitā*.

To be well able to awaken to and know the great affliction of birth and death is the meaning of *pāramitā*. That which was previously unawakened is now fully understood; this is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To be extensively able to manifest the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma is the meaning of *pāramitā*. Skillful...

The meaning of *pāramitā* is the removal of hindrances; the meaning of *pāramitā* is that giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, and so forth are performed without expectation of reward; the meaning of *pāramitā* is the thorough understanding of the realm of all sentient beings;
and the meaning of *pāramitā* is the fulfillment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The meaning of "honey" is the meaning of *pāramitā* as the attainment of non-retrogression; it is the meaning of *pāramitā* as the cultivation of a pure buddha-field;

it is the meaning of *pāramitā* as the maturation of sentient beings; it is the meaning of *pāramitā* as abiding at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and awakening to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
it is the meaning of *pāramitā* as the subduing of all Māras; it is the meaning of *pāramitā* as the accomplishment of all...
The meaning of *pāramitā* is the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes; the meaning of *pāramitā* is the destruction of all divergent views;
the meaning of *pāramitā* is the complete fulfillment of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities;
and the meaning of *pāramitā* is the accomplishment of the wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects.
“In this way, son of good family!
The meaning of the pāramitās is profoundly deep and immeasurable; I have merely explained it to you in brief.
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Siṃhavikrāntagāmin who rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
What has been explained above is profound and rare; the merits of all Buddhas are like nectar that satisfies all.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
“Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—whether they be devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans—as well as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who hear this sutra, they will certainly never again regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Why is this? O Devaputra!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who have planted the roots of virtue in past lives, they will be able to hear this sutra; it is not something that can be heard by those with meager merit."
If there are those who even briefly hear this sutra, read it, recite it, or transcribe it, these people, after casting off this body, will constantly behold all Buddhas.

Having seen the Buddhas, one is able to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma in their presence; one immediately attains the *dhāraṇī-seal of inexhaustibility*, as well as the *dhāraṇī for understanding the mental activities of all sentient beings*, the *dhāraṇī of the sun’s universal illumination*, the *dhāraṇī of pure stainlessness*, the *dhāraṇī of the immovability of all dharmas*, the *dhāraṇī of the indestructible vajra*, the *dhāraṇī for expounding the treasury of profound meanings*, the *dhāraṇī for skillfully understanding the languages of all sentient beings*, the *dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible seal of playful mastery in the stainless void*, and the *dhāraṇī of the emanation-bodies of all Buddhas*.
How much more so, then, for one who, having heard it, practices according to the teaching!

"Good son, if there is a bodhisattva who attains such a Dharma, they can manifest the body of a Buddha within all the buddha-fields of the ten directions to expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; yet they do not stir from the characteristics of phenomena, nor is there any coming or going."
Although they bring sentient beings to maturity, there are no sentient beings to be apprehended;
they constantly preach the Dharma, yet there is nothing preached;
they perpetually manifest birth, yet there is neither arising nor ceasing.
"Although they manifest coming and going, they possess no characteristics of coming or going.

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, three thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and immeasurable sentient beings all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Simhamati, along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, and non-humans, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Bodhicitta Spoken by the Buddha
